skyline.text: The made-up con­spir­acy the­ory that a lot of peo­ple be­lieved
Why Russia’s Spain-sized econ­omy can­not out­last the ad­vanced world
The re­fusal to flee Kyiv that turned the war around

brief.head: Black and white
brief.text: You don’t in­vade your neigh­bours, Ajay Shah said. Claiming Russia may in­vade Ukraine over the treaties it wants is as pre­pos­ter­ous as India in­vad­ing Bangladesh over treaties. {014-C02}

brief.head: Narrative beats truth
brief.text: Ajay Shah found Russian pro­pa­ganda on Indian out­lets. Amit Varma blamed media’s shift from jour­nal­ism to a con­tent game, in which the best pro­pa­ganda ma­chines win. {014-C07}

brief.head: Not stuck in the mud
brief.text: Many ex­pect the rasputitsa, the mud sea­son, to halt the fight­ing. But the south is warmer than Kyiv, Ajay Shah said, and win­ter wors­ens Russia’s prob­lems. {014-C17}

brief.head: The Finland tell
brief.text: Russia says it is fight­ing NATO. Yet with Finland now in NATO, Ajay Shah said, Russia’s force on the Finnish bor­der has fallen from 100 units to 20. {014-S11}

brief.head: The lab of war
brief.text: Western armies have never fought a peer with­out air su­pe­ri­or­ity, under skies full of enemy drones, Ajay Shah said. Now Ukraine knows more about con­ven­tional war than any­one. {014-C12}

thought.who: Amit Varma, recalling an old riddle about bacon and eggs to explain Ukraine’s morale

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah’s update on Ukraine, with Amit Varma
lead.head: No blitz, just a long squeeze

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 14

body: Ukraine’s sum­mer coun­terof­fen­sive has not pro­duced the ar­moured break­through that American an­a­lysts hoped for, and many have called it a fail­ure. Ajay Shah, back with Amit Varma for an up­date on the war, ar­gued that they are watch­ing the wrong game.

Varma began with the ob­vi­ous ques­tion: why should India care about a war so far away? Shah’s an­swer was his­tory. The de­feat of Nazi Germany and the col­lapse of the USSR, he said, brought a great flow­er­ing of free­dom, and Vladimir Putin wants to go back to a world where pow­er­ful coun­tries in­vade their neigh­bours.

If Russia wins, Shah said, Belarus and Poland could be next, and China might make a play for Taiwan or India. “Liberal democ­racy is a frag­ile com­pact,” he said, “and we need to renew our vows every day.” {014-C01}
## Weak strong­men
Many in the Indian mid­dle class, Shah said, re­spect strong­men and as­sume they build strong mil­i­taries. He ar­gued the re­verse.

In a lib­eral democ­racy, crit­ics out­side gov­ern­ment find its mis­takes and pro­pose fixes. Militaries are harder to crit­i­cise, be­cause of se­crecy and pa­tri­o­tism. Under an au­thor­i­tar­ian state the crit­ics are si­lenced and noth­ing is dis­closed.
“To un­der­stand a state is to un­der­stand that au­thor­i­tar­ian coun­tries make the worst mil­i­taries,” Shah said. {014-C05}
Varma saw the same rot in Russia’s failed in­va­sion: an age­ing au­to­crat sur­rounded by yes-men, his finest minds gone into exile, and delu­sions left un­chal­lenged.
## The see-through bat­tle­field

The bat­tle­field has changed too, Shah said. The long-heralded rev­o­lu­tion in mil­i­tary af­fairs is play­ing out fully in Ukraine, built on two things: drones, satel­lites and elec­tronic mon­i­tor­ing that make the bat­tle­field trans­par­ent, and pre­ci­sion mu­ni­tions that land within 10 or 20 me­tres.

That ends the old doc­trine of mass­ing force in se­cret for a break­through. Shah asked lis­ten­ers to “think of the foot­print that 100 ar­mored fight­ing ve­hi­cles and 1,000 peo­ple would leave in the eyes of a satel­lite”. {014-C09}

Western-style com­bined arms has a ceil­ing as well. Ukraine’s hastily trained civil­ians, Shah said, can make in­fantry, drones, ar­tillery and tanks work to­gether in groups of about 100, not 1,000.
So progress looks slow: by Shah’s count, Ukraine has crossed only about five of the 60 kilo­me­tres to the Sea of Azov.
## Grinding, not stalling

Attrition today, Shah ar­gued, is not the trench stale­mate of 1914 but Soviet-style deep op­er­a­tions. With NATO in­tel­li­gence, par­ti­sans and stand­off weapons such as Storm Shadow and HIMARS, Ukraine hits am­mu­ni­tion dumps, com­mand posts and sup­ply lines day after day.

Varma put it in chess terms. The Americans wanted Ukraine to at­tack like Tal or Fischer; Ukraine is play­ing like Capablanca or Karpov. “You can never say in ad­vance what is going to break where,” he said, “but you have to just keep ping­ing away and some­thing or the other will break.” {014-C15}

Ukraine’s real war econ­omy, Shah said, is the whole ad­vanced world, with South Korea the most im­por­tant maker of the ar­tillery shells it re­ceives. Russia, with a Spain-sized GDP, loses about 1,000 tanks a year and makes about 200.
“Once you start think­ing that wars are won by economies and not by mil­i­taries,” he said, “then it’s clear as day.” {014-C16}
So Ukraine can af­ford to waste equip­ment, but stays fru­gal with lives. The open ques­tion, Shah said, is whether Russia will find “Stalin lev­els of re­solve” in cop­ing with its losses.
His ver­dict on the coun­terof­fen­sive was brief: “It ain’t done.”

second.label: Energy war
second.head: The gas bluff, called
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how Europe beat Russia’s energy blackmail, and what it cost Moscow

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on how Europe beat the energy blackmail

body: Vladimir Putin bet that cut­ting gas to Europe would cause a deep re­ces­sion and work­ing-class anger, feed­ing com­mu­nists and Nazis and break­ing Europe’s cen­trist coali­tions. “We’ve seen that movie a hun­dred years ago,” Ajay Shah said.

Instead, Europe tripled its work on re­new­ables, im­ported LNG from all over the world and pro­tected poor house­holds from the price rise. “Before the war, peo­ple be­lieved that it takes two to three years to build an LNG ter­mi­nal,” Shah said. “They got LNG ter­mi­nals done in six months.” {014-S02}

Calling the bluff cost Russia its main buyer, Shah said, and its econ­omy had been built on sell­ing gas cheaply to Europe. {#gas} The ad­vanced economies, he said, are easy to un­der­es­ti­mate from a dis­tance.

quote.text: There are going to be books and books writ­ten about how Europe fought that en­ergy black­mail of 2022.

third.head: Every front, all at once

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Stalin’s choice not to concentrate

body: After Operation Barbarossa in June 1941, Ajay Shah said, three German army groups ad­vanced along a very long front in the USSR, to­wards St Petersburg, Moscow and later Stalingrad and the oil fields of Baku. {014-S08}

Stalin had to choose: mass his forces for one break­through, or fight in many places. Shah counts him, like Lenin and Trotsky, among the so­phis­ti­cated in­tel­lec­tu­als of the era. Stalin knew the USSR had the big­ger pop­u­la­tion, and that with American in­dus­try be­hind it, it would out­pro­duce Germany.
So he counter-attacked ev­ery­where, to wear down German men and in­dus­try. Germany could not be strong ev­ery­where, which is part of why it lost Stalingrad.
Shah’s sum­mary: “You can’t pre­dict where it will break, but it’ll break some­where.” {#somewhere} That, he said, is the in­tu­ition for think­ing about Ukraine today.

box.title: The man in the Kremlin
box.text: Ajay Shah calls Vladimir Putin a KGB man “brought up in the dark arts”, who sees the USSR’s col­lapse as a tragedy. Amit Varma saw in the failed in­va­sion the mega­lo­ma­nia of a 70-year-old who han­kers for em­pire. {#megalomania}

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.head: A faraway war, close to home
sections.caption: why a faraway war matters
body: Why should any­one in India care about a war in some other ran­dom place? Amit Varma put the ques­tion, and Ajay Shah an­swered with his­tory.

The great drama of the 20th cen­tury, Shah said, ended with the col­lapse of Nazi Germany and the USSR, and a great flow­er­ing of free­dom. Vladimir Putin seeks to go back to a world where pow­er­ful coun­tries in­vade their neigh­bours.

Varma re­called Thomas Jefferson’s line that lib­erty re­quires eter­nal vig­i­lance, and the hope cap­tured by Francis Fukuyama’s essay *The End of History?*, which re­cent years have shaken. {014-R10}

The rise of Trump, Xi Jinping, Putin and Erdogan, Shah said, raises the stakes: right-wing au­thor­i­tar­i­ans prop each other up, as Mussolini, Hitler and Imperial Japan did. Going up­stream from Hemingway’s *For Whom the Bell Tolls*, he said, the world could not ig­nore Spain in 1936, and can­not ig­nore Ukraine now. {014-C01}
## The state is not the peo­ple

Varma urged lis­ten­ers to sep­a­rate Russia from the Russian peo­ple. Some 40 grand­mas­ters, es­sen­tially the country’s top chess play­ers, wrote a let­ter protest­ing against the in­va­sion, and many had to leave Russia. The one ex­cep­tion he named, Sergey Karyakin, he called a cow­ard. {014-S04}
For Shah, it was Garry Kasparov who showed him that Putin was not just one more Russian strong­man. {#kasparov}
~ When a state in­vades an­other coun­try, the hosts said, ral­ly­ing around the flag is a basic in­tel­lec­tual blun­der. Protest, Varma said, is the pa­tri­otic act.

quote.text: In my mind, there’s a sim­ple line, which is you don’t in­vade your neigh­bors.

sections.label: The dark arts
sections.head: Yes-men make poor generals
sections.caption: why the invasion itself failed
body: Almost ev­ery­one, Amit Varma said, ex­pected Russia’s in­va­sion to suc­ceed and its oc­cu­pa­tion to fail. As Michael Kofman put it in an in­ter­view Varma had read, the sur­prise was that the in­va­sion it­self failed.

The Russians had as­sumed they would be wel­comed with open arms. Big armies, like big com­pa­nies, can os­sify and pass in­for­ma­tion slowly from bot­tom to top. And au­thor­i­tar­ian lead­ers, Varma said, “get sur­rounded by yes men. And no one dares to con­tra­dict them in any way.” {014-C04}
Their finest minds go into exile, and delu­sions per­sist.
## Empire by stealth

Ajay Shah sees Vladimir Putin as a KGB man with a sus­pi­cious na­tion­al­ism, who openly calls the USSR’s col­lapse a great geopo­lit­i­cal tragedy. Shah counts that col­lapse among the most glo­ri­ous mo­ments of the 20th cen­tury.

Putin is re­build­ing an em­pire step by step, Shah said. Land is grabbed, fake re­publics such as the DPR and LPR are set up, and the Russian army fights in dis­guise in what is passed off as a civil war: the “stan­dard Hitler-Stalin play­book”.

Behind it is the civil­i­sa­tional state, which re­jects na­tional bor­ders. By that logic, Shah said, a state could claim the Chinese in Malaysia are op­pressed and in­vade Malaysia to help them. {014-C03}
~ The bor­ders be­tween India and Bangladesh, and be­tween China and India, are in­vi­o­lable, Shah said.

quote.text: There is a phrase for it, it’s called civ­i­liza­tional state. The civ­i­liza­tional state is a truly dan­ger­ous con­cept.

sections.label: Incentives
sections.head: Ego versus existence
sections.caption: morale and authoritarian militaries
body: Amit Varma reached for an old rid­dle. When it comes to bacon and eggs, what is the dif­fer­ence be­tween the chicken and the pig? “The chicken is in­volved, but the pig is com­mit­ted.” {014-C08}
Russia, he said, is fight­ing for the delu­sions of one mega­lo­ma­niac at the top. Ukraine is fight­ing for its ex­is­tence.

Ajay Shah agreed that morale is an im­mense edge: war, he said, is about “money, men, ma­te­rial, and morale”. But Czechoslovakia and Austria were over­run all the same. You may fight as des­per­ately as you can, Shah said, “but there are no guar­an­tees”. {#guarantees}
## Three lev­els of trou­ble

Shah then set out three lev­els of gov­er­nance. Civilian gov­ern­ment in a lib­eral democ­racy is eas­i­est: if ev­ery­one at­tacks the Bank of England every day, the bugs get fixed. Militaries are harder, be­cause se­crecy and pa­tri­o­tism mute crit­i­cism. Worst of all is the mil­i­tary of an au­thor­i­tar­ian state, where crit­ics are si­lenced and there is no mar­ket test.

The United States dis­closes how many ar­tillery shells and Javelin mis­siles it bought in which year. “In the Indian bud­get, you get noth­ing,” Shah said. He finds Japan’s mil­i­tary eas­ier to study than India’s.
~ Transparency, Varma added, in­di­cates ac­count­abil­ity, and ac­count­abil­ity in­di­cates ef­fi­ciency. {014-C05}

quote.text: In the United States, you will get the pre­cise fis­cal data for how many ar­tillery shells were pro­duced in which year.

sections.label: The new warfare
sections.head: Aim at Andheri, hit Bandra
sections.caption: the revolution in military affairs
body: A tank on today’s bat­tle­field, Amit Varma said, can be de­tected and de­stroyed within ten min­utes. Ukraine was using about 10,000 drones a month, by older es­ti­mates, many of them cheap Chinese-made ones. {#drones}

Ajay Shah or­gan­ised the his­tory in phases: Napoleonic war­fare; the First World War stale­mate, bro­ken by com­bined arms; the in­ter­war work on tanks and air­craft by Marshal Tukhachevsky and German thinkers; then a long nu­clear de­tour.
By the 1980s and 1990s peo­ple spoke of a rev­o­lu­tion in mil­i­tary af­fairs, to the ir­ri­ta­tion of old-timers. In Ukraine, Shah said, it is play­ing out fully for the first time. {#rma}
## Thousands of bombs, one fac­tory

It rests on bat­tle­field trans­parency, from drones, satel­lites and elec­tronic mon­i­tor­ing, and on pre­ci­sion. In the Second World War, half the bombs landed more than one or five kilo­me­tres from the tar­get. {#bombs}
“So if some­one tries to bomb me in Andheri,” Varma said, “they’ll get you in Bandra.” {014-J02}

Errors of 10 or 20 me­tres are now in­creas­ingly com­mon, so force massed in se­cret can be seen and hit. Varma noted that one his­to­rian traces the American doc­trine of con­cen­trated force to Ulysses S. Grant. {014-J12}
~ The Americans ex­pected Ukraine’s coun­terof­fen­sive to fight that way, Varma said, and were dis­ap­pointed when it did not.

quote.text: And all you need is 10 ar­tillery shells with clus­ter mu­ni­tion to make a very bad day for that force.

sections.label: The front
sections.head: Too obvious to be the plan
sections.caption: the map, and the limits of combined arms
body: Ajay Shah walked lis­ten­ers through the map. Without the Kerch Bridge, he said, Crimea has no land con­nec­tion to Russia. {#kerch}

The oc­cu­pied south is sup­plied out of Crimea, so every arm­chair strate­gist dreamt of one ar­moured thrust of about 60 to 65 kilo­me­tres to the Sea of Azov. Shah was sus­pi­cious. “If some­thing is so ob­vi­ous, you can’t be doing that.” {014-J07}

Amit Varma of­fered von Moltke and Mike Tyson on plans. Shah of­fered a bor­rowed line: “The plan is use­less. The plan­ning is ev­ery­thing.” What mod­ern mil­i­taries need, he said, is “to be able to learn, im­pro­vise, and adapt under fire”. {014-C10}
## Two and two make twenty-two

Western com­bined arms asks in­fantry, drones, elec­tronic war­fare, ar­tillery and tanks to work as one, which takes years of train­ing and life-or-death trust. Pettiness gets in the way. The elec­tronic war­fare man, in Shah’s sketch, tells the drone man: “You guys, you just fly these birds. We shoot them down.” {014-J06}
Ukraine’s hastily trained civil­ians, Shah said, have man­aged it in groups of about 100, and fum­bled above that. {014-C11}
~ Western doc­trine also as­sumes total air su­pe­ri­or­ity, he said, and has never faced enemy drones or a peer. Ukraine has.

quote.text: I think that war is the lab where the next gen­er­a­tion of the Western way of war is being forged.

sections.label: The masterpiece
sections.head: Economies, not armies, win
sections.caption: the long war and its economics
body: America’s way of war, Ajay Shah said, was built around its in­dus­trial might and pop­u­la­tion. The giant slum­bered until 1941, then built the world’s big­gest tank fac­to­ries from scratch. By early 1944, field com­man­ders were say­ing they did not want any more tanks. {014-S06}

Churchill, lead­ing a coun­try with far fewer peo­ple to lose, kept hold­ing the Americans back. History, Shah said, will judge him kindly. {014-S07} A smaller na­tion fights more cau­tiously, as Ukraine does with its sol­diers.
## Quiet be­fore the col­lapse

Ukraine’s gains at Kherson and Kharkiv also looked like fruit­less at­tacks for a while, Shah said. Under the hood, Russia was los­ing its abil­ity to sup­ply Kherson, until one day it sim­ply left. {014-S10}

The thrust to the Sea of Azov was re­ally about lo­gis­tics. HIMARS, with a range of about 30 kilo­me­tres, could not reach the M14 high­way. Ukraine need only creep close enough, with bet­ter stand­off weapons. {014-C14}
Shah dis­missed Russia as “Saudi Arabia with nukes”, a Spain-sized econ­omy fac­ing the com­bined ad­vanced world. {014-J05}
~ Even its force on the Finnish bor­der, he said, has shrunk to a fifth of its tra­di­tional size.

quote.text: They’ve got to get close enough for their stand­off weapons to dis­rupt Russian lo­gis­tics. And that’s not as hard as it seems.
In fact, if our coun­try does some­thing wrong or if our gov­ern­ment does some­thing wrong, it is a sign of your pa­tri­o­tism that you protest for the sake of what your coun­try means to you.

p3.title: War and other stories
p3.deck: Four tales told in the episode, from Kyiv to a manga master’s deathbed

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the moment the West changed its mind
stories.head: Offered a lift, he stayed put
body: Russia’s in­tel­li­gence as­sess­ment, Ajay Shah said, was that a show of force would be enough. The West would buckle, and with­out Western sup­port the Ukrainian army would flee. It would be like Afghanistan, where the Taliban won the mo­ment the Americans left.

Vladimir Putin had his rea­sons. Russia in­vaded Georgia on 8 August 2008, and no­body helped. In February 2014 he grabbed Crimea, and no­body did any­thing. “And so he started get­ting com­fort­able that the West does not have a stom­ach for a fight,” Shah said. {014-S03}

Russia had not even done the full mil­i­tary plan­ning for an in­va­sion. Amit Varma re­called a clumsy land­ing at the air­port in Kyiv, and dif­fer­ent groups sent to as­sas­si­nate Volodymyr Zelensky. “Thankfully they failed,” he said. {#assassins}
Then came what Shah called a price­less mo­ment. The Americans of­fered Zelensky a flight out of Kyiv, ex­actly what they had done in Afghanistan.

“And Zelensky said, I don’t want a ride, I want am­mu­ni­tion,” Shah said. “That’s just one of the most price­less mo­ments in world his­tory, where he said, No, this is my coun­try. I will stand and fight.” {014-S01}
Everything started chang­ing around that, Shah said. Zelensky ral­lied his peo­ple, and the West turned around and said it would sup­port Ukraine.

~ Shah likened it to 1939. Hitler had moved on Austria and Czechoslovakia, but when he in­vaded Poland on 1 September, England and France said enough is enough, and gave him an ul­ti­ma­tum to with­draw.
stories.why: Putin’s plan rested on an as­sump­tion about will: that no­body would stand and fight. One leader’s re­fusal to run broke it. Aggression that goes un­pun­ished teaches the ag­gres­sor the wrong les­son, and ap­pease­ment tends to end abruptly.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Zelensky’s refusal to flee

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why Ukraine fought for Bakhmut
stories.head: Lost the town, broke Wagner
body: Bakhmut, which Ajay Shah called a dinky town of 70,000 peo­ple, was taken by Wagner. Simplistic think­ing says Ukraine should have re­treated early. Retreat to where? “Cities are where you do the de­fense,” Shah said. {#dinky}

So Ukraine fought a long fight­ing re­treat. “By and large, Ukraine lost,” Shah said. “But in the process of los­ing, they in­flicted so much dam­age upon Wagner that it trig­gered off the mutiny by Wagner.” {014-S09}

Like Stalingrad, Bakhmut be­came a sym­bol. Losing ground that Prigozhin and Utkin had con­quered would be a PR dis­as­ter for Russia’s de­fence min­istry, so it pours forces in to hold it, and Ukraine keeps press­ing.
~ “So you’ve al­ways got to count the ex­change rate,” Shah said: how many tanks, and how many peo­ple, each side loses.
stories.why: A town lost can still be a bat­tle won. Count the ex­change rate of losses, not just kilo­me­tres gained, and watch for sym­bols: a place that be­comes one can turn into a trap that drains the enemy.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the fighting retreat at Bakhmut

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a conspiracy theory invented on purpose
stories.head: Never seen a baby pigeon?
body: Amit Varma asked Ajay Shah if he had heard of Peter McIndoe. Shah had not. At 23, Varma said, McIndoe de­cided as a pub­lic ex­per­i­ment to give birth to a con­spir­acy the­ory: birds aren’t real.
Decades ago, the the­ory went, the US gov­ern­ment killed mil­lions of birds and re­placed them with ro­bots that spy on civil­ians. Why do birds sit on power lines? They are recharg­ing.
“Have you ever seen a baby pi­geon?” Varma asked. “It’s be­cause only adult pi­geons are cre­ated in the fac­to­ries.” {014-S05} And why do birds poop on peo­ple? To track them.
~ McIndoe knew it was un­true, but many peo­ple be­lieved him. For three years he kept up the cha­rade, driv­ing around in a van and hand­ing out fly­ers. {#van}
stories.why: Belief is eas­ily man­u­fac­tured: a made-up the­ory, a few mock proofs and a van full of fly­ers were enough for many peo­ple. Varma called it a de­light­ful story, told after Shah de­scribed skies full of enemy drones.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the birds that aren’t real

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the manga master who drew to the end
stories.head: Let me work, said the master
body: “Tezuka was like a god for me,” wrote Yoshihiro Tatsumi of Osamu Tezuka, in a pas­sage Amit Varma read out. {014-J18}

The young ad­mirer went on to pi­o­neer gekiga, dark urban sto­ries that were a re­ac­tion against manga. The mas­ter, Varma said, was taken by it, cham­pi­oned the new form and, around 1970, wrote *Ode to Kirihito* in its spirit.

Tezuka worked con­stantly all his life. In 1989 he died of stom­ach can­cer. In hos­pi­tal he kept try­ing to draw, and a nurse came to take his draw­ing equip­ment away. “And his last words were, I’m beg­ging you, let me work,” Varma said. {014-S12}
~ After his death, his daugh­ter opened his drawer at home and found a whole bunch of un­fin­ished work. Varma found it in­spir­ing.
stories.why: A mas­ter hum­ble enough to learn from a young ad­mirer, and de­voted to his craft to his hos­pi­tal bed. Varma, rec­om­mend­ing *Ode to Kirihito*, called it one of the most pow­er­ful graphic nov­els he has read. {014-R04}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Osamu Tezuka’s last words

quiz.a: He said he did not want a ride; he wanted am­mu­ni­tion.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s war arithmetic, what multiplication factor does Russian incompetence apply?
quiz.a: About 0.33, which makes the two sides roughly equal in bat­tle.

quiz.q: Above roughly what group size have Ukraine’s hastily trained forces fumbled at combined arms?
quiz.a: About 100 peo­ple; a thou­sand can­not yet be made to work to­gether.

quiz.q: Before the war, how long was an LNG terminal thought to take, and how long did Europe take?
quiz.a: Two to three years was the be­lief; Europe did it in six months.

quiz.q: Which chess players did Amit Varma say Ukraine is playing like, rather than Tal or Fischer?
quiz.a: Capablanca and Karpov, the po­si­tional mas­ters who wait for chances to ap­pear.

quiz.q: What were Osamu Tezuka’s last words, as Amit Varma told the story?
quiz.a: “I’m beg­ging you, let me work,” as a nurse came to take his equip­ment.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 14. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Volodymyr Zelenskyy (Press Service of the President of Ukraine, CC BY 4.0); Vladimir Putin (Пресс-служба Президента России, CC BY 4.0); Winston Churchill (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Osamu Tezuka (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Francis Fukuyama (Gobierno de Chile, CC BY 2.0); Lawrence Freedman (Chatham House, CC BY 2.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A five-and-a-half-hour mas­ter­class from Ajay on the war and the deep his­to­ries of Russia and Ukraine, built on a life­time of read­ing and a counter to Russian pro­pa­ganda.

shelf.title: Russia, Ukraine, Foreign Policy (Episode 268 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane and Nitin Pai
shelf.why: Pranay Kotasthane and Nitin Pai on Europe’s dis­as­trous re­liance on Russian pipe­lines in­stead of di­ver­si­fy­ing sup­ply, and their fear, later borne out, that the gas de­pen­dence could be used as a weapon.

shelf.title: How the War Was Won
shelf.creator: Phillips Payson O’Brien
shelf.why: A re­cent book of­fer­ing new in­sights on the grunt on the ground ver­sus the high eco­nomic strat­egy of the Second World War.

shelf.title: Ode to Kirihito
shelf.creator: Osamu Tezuka
shelf.why: One of the most pow­er­ful graphic nov­els he has read: an odyssey into the human con­di­tion and the moral decay cir­cum­stances can bring.

shelf.title: The Push Man and Other Stories
shelf.creator: Yoshihiro Tatsumi
shelf.why: Gekiga at its best: dark urban sto­ries that stare into the depths of the human soul and go where manga doesn’t, in the vein Goya opened up cen­turies ear­lier.

shelf.title: Abandon the Old in Tokyo
shelf.creator: Yoshihiro Tatsumi
shelf.why: More bleak, un­for­get­table gekiga with end­ings you have to read for your­self.

shelf.title: Birds Aren’t Real? How a Conspiracy Takes Flight
shelf.creator: Peter McIndoe
shelf.why: A de­light­ful first-hand ac­count of how a de­lib­er­ately in­vented con­spir­acy the­ory gets peo­ple to be­lieve it.

shelf.title: An Interview with Mike Kofman
shelf.creator: Lawrence Freedman
shelf.why: Kofman cap­tures what sur­prised ev­ery­one: the oc­cu­pa­tion was al­ways ex­pected to fail, but al­most no­body ex­pected the in­va­sion it­self to fail.

shelf.title: The hard lessons from Ukraine’s summer offensive
shelf.creator: Christopher Miller and Ben Hall (Financial Times)
shelf.why: It vividly de­scribes the coun­terof­fen­sive as ‘a war of tree lines’: small in­fantry groups ad­vanc­ing field by field under ar­tillery and drones, slowly wear­ing down Russian de­fences.

shelf.title: The End of History?
shelf.creator: Francis Fukuyama
shelf.why: Fukuyama’s essay cap­tures the post-1989 be­lief that lib­eral democ­racy had won the ar­gu­ment for good.

shelf.title: The Battle of Kursk
shelf.why: Russia’s de­fences today come straight from that Soviet play­book, and Ukraine has so far cut through only one to one-and-a-half of three or four lines.

shelf.title: DeepStateMap (live Ukraine war map)
shelf.creator: DeepStateMap
shelf.why: The ge­og­ra­phy and lo­gis­tics of the front only make sense when you can see them.

shelf.title: The Problem (Washington Post on the Melitopol counteroffensive)
shelf.creator: The Washington Post
shelf.why: Background on the chal­lenge of Ukraine’s push to­ward Melitopol and the Sea of Azov.

shelf.title: Basic facts about the map (NYT interactive)
shelf.creator: The New York Times
shelf.why: A vis­ual primer on the counteroffensive’s ge­og­ra­phy.

shelf.title: Ukraine’s offensive: is it failing?
shelf.creator: Lawrence Freedman
shelf.why: Takes on the dis­ap­point­ment that the coun­terof­fen­sive hasn’t pro­duced a quick break­through.

shelf.title: Perseverance and Adaptation: Ukraine’s Counteroffensive at Three Months
shelf.creator: Michael Kofman and Rob Lee (War on the Rocks)
shelf.why: A three-month as­sess­ment of how the coun­terof­fen­sive is going.

shelf.title: Stalemate, Zugzwang and a long Middle Game
shelf.creator: Lawrence Freedman
shelf.why: Freedman’s take on whether the war is a stale­mate, in the same chess-flavoured terms the hosts use.

shelf.title: Conflict in Ukraine: A timeline (2014 – present)
shelf.creator: Nigel Walker (House of Commons Library)
shelf.why: A chronol­ogy of the con­flict since Crimea in 2014.

shelf.creator: RUSI

laughs.text: After Amit re­lays how Gaurav Chintamani was mind-blown by Ajay’s five-hour Ukraine mas­ter­class, Ajay de­flects: ‘I only know 16 things.’
On WWII bombs land­ing kilo­me­tres off tar­get, Amit says: ‘So if some­one tries to bomb me in Andheri, they’ll get you in Bandra.’
Ajay’s war math: Russia has three times Ukraine’s econ­omy and pop­u­la­tion, ‘And Russian in­com­pe­tence is like a 0.33 mul­ti­pli­ca­tion fac­tor. So the two sides are roughly equal in bat­tle.’
Ajay’s one-line ver­dict on Russia’s econ­omy: ‘It is Saudi Arabia with nukes.’

Ajay on ri­valry be­tween spe­cial­ists: the drone guy boasts that fly­ing a drone is the great­est skill in the world, and the elec­tronic war­fare guy replies, ‘Yeah, you guys, you just fly these birds. We, we shoot them down.’

On the dag­ger thrust to the Sea of Azov, ‘dreamt up in pub­lic do­main by every arm­chair mil­i­tary strate­gist in the whole world’, Ajay re­marks: ‘if some­thing is so ob­vi­ous, you can’t be doing that.’
Amit on Tezuka being called both the fa­ther and the god­fa­ther of manga: ‘So fa­ther and god­fa­ther at the same time.’
Two quotes on plans from Amit: von Moltke’s ‘no plan sur­vives con­tact with the enemy’ and Mike Tyson’s ‘Everyone has a plan till they get punched in the face.’

Ulysses S. Grant as the source of the American doc­trine of con­cen­trated force. Amit quotes a WWII his­to­rian: ‘They built a pow­er­ful army when the need arose, at­tacked the enemy’s strength as quickly as pos­si­ble, and took and in­flicted ca­su­al­ties until he stopped strug­gling. Anything less was a dis­trac­tion.’ He also cites Lawrence Freedman’s sum­mary of US doc­trine as a ‘main effort’ on a sin­gle front.
Amit’s chess pan­theon: Capablanca and Karpov as po­si­tional mas­ters, Tal and Fischer as at­tack­ers, and Kasparov’s com­pli­ment that Carlsen is a com­bi­na­tion of Fischer and Karpov.
Judo, Putin’s favourite sport, where the pa­tient, nim­ble fighter beats the strong one. Amit de­lights that Ukraine is win­ning the judo match against Russia.
Gekiga, the dark, adult, urban comics move­ment Yoshihiro Tatsumi pi­o­neered against cheerier manga. Tatsumi wrote of Tezuka: ‘Tezuka was like a god for me.’
